item.title: MP calls for action after her likeness used for AI porn deepfakes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and impactful

MP calls for action after her likeness used for AI porn deepfakes

A member of parliament whose name and image were used in AI content on porn sites said the issue could make women less likely to want to enter public life.

Mims Davies, the shadow Welsh Secretary, said she received an email in her parliamentary inbox which said "her likeness was found on forums in abusive and pornographic content".

The Conservative frontbencher said people making money from deepfakes was "grotesque", urging people to report it if it happens to them so that "culprits can be held to account".

"It's completely unacceptable, it's a violation and an outrage," she told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.

Deepfakes are videos, pictures or audio clips made with artificial intelligence to look real.

It is illegal, external to share or threaten to share intimate photos or videos of someone without their consent, including through deepfake images.

Davies said she had waived her right to anonymity to call for more resources to find and prosecute culprits.

Ofcom, the communications regulator, said "significant action is being taken to tackle intimate image abuse" but added there was "more to do".

Davies, MP for East Grinstead and Uckfield in East Sussex, said: "There are things you expect to be dealing with these days in public life and frankly this is not it.

"This could be any woman. This could be anyone in politics, in business, or down in your high street.

"We need to be able to protect ourselves from deepfakes."

She added: "This is going to have an effect on our daily lives, on our lifestyles. We need an answer to this.

"There's a problem, a new frontier which we need to battle."

She previously told the BBC she was spiked on a night out in 2019.

Mims Davies: My likeness was found in abusive and pornographic content

Shadow Welsh Secretary Mims Davies says her name and image were used on porn sites without her consent, and warns it's putting women off entering politics.

Davies, who studied politics and international relations at Swansea University before embarking on a career in journalism in Wales, said the issue was likely to make women "feel less likely to want to enter public life".

"It doesn't just affect you personally, it affects families. You never know when you're walking into a room what people might be thinking.

"We need more women in public life at every single level, from councillors, to Westminster and to the Senedd. It's tough out there.

"We need those kinds of voices in the room."

Her office confirmed reports have been made to the Metropolitan Police and parliamentary authorities.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: "Nobody should have to experience the trauma of having an explicit deepfake created or shared without their consent.

"Under the Online Safety Act, tech firms must assess and mitigate the risk of UK users encountering illegal content like this on their sites and apps, and remove it quickly when they become aware of it.

"We've laid down clear expectations for how platforms should do this â including by using automated technology to deal with illegal intimate images â and we've driven some of the strongest changes of any online safety regulation in the world.

"We've also shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

In January, Ofcom launched an investigation into X over concerns its AI tool Grok was being used to create sexualised images.

The regulator gave platforms until the end of September this year to take effective steps to stop illegal intimate images and deepfakes from spreading.

At the time, it warned that any firms which breached their duties would face fines of up to 10% of their global annual revenue.

item.title: Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, significant political impact

Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU

Nigel Farage has helped launch a new campaign against the UK rejoining the European Union.

The Reform UK leader offered his support to Keep Britain Out, which sees him reunite with his Brexit-supporting ally Arron Banks - who co-founded the Leave.EU campaign during the 2016 referendum.

Farage was the first MP to sign the campaign's "Pledge for Britain". This contains "10 commitments" for elected officials to abide by, including opposing rejoining the EU, its single market or customs union.

The campaign was launched as Prime Minister Andy Burnham explores closer ties with the EU, after he agreed a deal with the bloc covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good" and has suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

But he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

On Monday, Burnham said there was "no fixed destination" on the talks with the EU, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, Farage said the 2016 referendum was the "most divisive thing I have seen in families, in communities" and he hopes the next general election "kills this stone dead".

He told reporters: "I didn't pick this fight, the prime minister has picked this fight. As far as I was concerned it was done and dusted.

"But if battle has to be joined I will join it gleefully. What he's doing is madness, it's not necessary."

Farage said Keep Britain Out would be a "forward-looking, positive campaign about how Britain can be richer, more productive" outside the EU.

There are 10 issues listed on the pledge card, including asking signatories to "oppose mass migration" and support the country's farming and fishing industries.

Farage suggested he expects other Reform MPs and candidates to sign the pledges.

Banks said he wants pro-leave MPs to support them, adding: "We hope some Labour MPs will see sense and sign it and even Conservatives."

Asked if he is funding the campaign and to what extent, Banks said a "whole series of donors" have been "back in touch".

He added: "The last campaign was also funded by the British public, so I'm not going to go into who's donating what at this stage."

The launch of Keep Britain Out follows the formation of another anti-EU campaign called Stay Out, which has received support from Lord Gove - the chairman of the Vote Leave campaign in 2016.

Meanwhile, the European Movement is helping launch a rival campaign to rejoin the EU, called Get In.

item.title: The Contract Was the Easy Part: How Accelerator Day Put the Pentagon on the Clock
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail, strategic insight

go beyond the headlines.

November 25, 2026

Cara Teeter and Bonnie Evangelista

The Pentagon demands urgency from industry while allowing its own decisions to drift. On July 24, we ran an accelerator day to put the government under a deadline and make it responsible for what followed. We led the inaugural event for the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict, assembling the process in less than two months and executing $650,000 in legally binding awards over eight hours.

Each of the 15 finalists received $10,000 for its technical “pitch” to the government assessment team. 10 received an additional $50,000 in seed funding to advance toward operational assessment, the subsequent phase of activity called “Gate 2.” Those amounts support an initial commitment to the next phase. The total cost of a useful assessment would depend on the technology, mission, and operating environment. We also assigned each advancing company a government project manager responsible for scoping the work, arranging funds, and bringing end users and potential adopters into it.

We started small so we could learn before committing substantially more money, then modify or end investment as evidence warranted. That portfolio approach preserves options as threats and technologies change. Its credibility depends on the government’s willingness to carry those decisions through assessment, and where justified, into fielding and sustainment.

Pentagon news and Breaking Defense covered the event and its ambition to accelerate contracting. Three months later, we can describe the decisions made after the awards and what work remains. Our experience exposes a harder test for acquisition transformation: whether the government can sustain its urgency once the event ends and the coordination becomes difficult.

In its 2026 annual assessment, the Government Accountability Office reported that the average time for major defense acquisition programs to deliver capability had exceeded 12 years and was likely to increase. It also found continued shortfalls in applying iterative development practices. Those timelines encompass requirements, development, testing, and production decisions far beyond the scope of our prototype awards. However, those timelines establish the institutional context for why the department needs faster ways to assess mature commercial technologies.

Our contribution to this problem will depend on bringing operational learning forward and finding organizations prepared to act on it. An assessment can expose a technical limitation, reveal a better application, or show that a proposed solution deserves no further funding. Reaching those judgments early gives acquisition leaders room to change course before a program’s commitments become difficult to unwind.

As one of us argued previously in these pages, acquisition incentives often make visible failure more consequential than delay. Another review can feel safer than authorizing an assessment that would answer an unresolved question. We designed accelerator day to force a decision while the operational need was immediate, with leaders, funding, and contracting support available to act. The same demand for a timely decision should now follow every project beyond its initial award. If not, operators bear the cost of waiting while responsibility disperses across the organizations processing the request.

We worked with operational partners to frame nine challenge areas, issued a call for solutions, reviewed nearly 700 submissions, and selected 15 finalists for accelerator day. We transferred funding to Army Contracting Command-Rock Island and assembled multi-disciplinary assessment teams before the pitches began. Industry received operational problems and room to propose applications of technology that companies had already built. Advancement depended on whether there was sufficient operational demand to justify a proposed solution.

We used One Nation Innovation’s Open National Innovation Exchange other transaction vehicle, a flexible agreement mechanism for prototype work. One Nation Innovation serves as an acquisition intermediary connecting government and industry through a digital marketplace. The instrument let us tailor the initial business arrangement to the limited work and modest commitment involved while preserving flexibility for subsequent investment. We kept the terms simple and proportional to that stage, avoiding lengthy negotiations and complexity that the initial awards did not require.

Giving industry that latitude has a basis beyond this event. A 2025 study in the Journal of Political Economy compared Air Force research competitions that allowed firms to propose ideas to competitions that prescribed desired products. The researchers found that awards under the open approach increased commercial innovation and military technology adoption. Although those findings support seeking industry proposals for operational needs, our particular model still should establish its value through results.

Our assessment teams combined operational users, technical and acquisition experts, allied-partner representatives, and strategic stakeholders. Participants came from the Army and Navy, the department’s research and engineering organization, Cyber Command, special operations organizations, and the Department of Homeland Security and Veterans Affairs. Every evaluator signed a nondisclosure agreement and was required to disclose actual or potential conflicts before assessing vendor pitches.…

item.title: Does Congress Really Want Its War Powers Back?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, legal and political analysis

go beyond the headlines.

Elizabeth Beavers

November 25, 2026

Congress wants its war powers back. At least, that is the message that the legislature has communicated to the public numerous times over the past decade. Members of Congress have forced an astonishing number of votes on resolutions challenging unauthorized presidential warmaking, with some achieving historically unprecedented success in one or both chambers of Congress. But soon, it will become time for Congress to put its money where its mouth is.

In its flurry of Vietnam War-era reforms in the 1970s, Congress enacted the War Powers Resolution as a framework to manage the divided war powers that the Constitution gives to both the legislature and the commander in chief. The law was enacted over President Richard Nixon’s veto, and sought to clarify and limit the circumstances under which presidents could utilize military force without congressional acquiescence. Further, it enacted requirements to increase presidential reporting to and consultation with Congress. Post-Nixon presidents have expressed doubts about and outright opposition to various aspects of these provisions’ constitutionality.

In addition to those features, this statutory scheme reserved to Congress the power to pass resolutions overriding presidents when they deployed military force without congressional authorization. These resolutions were “privileged,” meaning any member of Congress could force a debate and vote on them.

Originally, war powers resolutions were meant to become binding upon passage through Congress. However, in 1983, the Supreme Court ruled in its landmark case INS v. Chadha that so-called “legislative vetoes” were unconstitutional unless they were presented to the president for signature. But, of course, this tool was created for Congress to oppose the president, and so any passed resolutions presented to the president would inevitably be vetoed. Thus, it appeared that unless Congress could muster the two-thirds supermajority required to overcome a presidential veto, they would amount to nothing more than press releases.

Yet members of Congress keep introducing and voting on them. In a forthcoming study, I track congressional use of resolutions eligible for expedited procedures, either as a concurrent resolution under section 5(c) of the House of Representatives or as a joint resolution in the Senate utilizing the post-Chadha amended procedures represented in Section 601(b) of the International Security Assistance and Arms Export Control Act of 1976.

According to my calculations, members of Congress have introduced 89 of these resolutions and forced votes on 45 of them since Chadha. This number tabulates how many privileged war powers resolutions have been considered on the floor of Congress in any manner, including procedural votes. Far and away, the Trump administration’s unauthorized military actions in Iran have prompted the most resolutions, to the tune of 39 introduced and 15 receiving votes thus far. In a historic development earlier this year, one passed both the House and the Senate in its original form as a concurrent resolution that section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution sought to make binding on the president without his signature pre-Chadha. Although two others have passed the House of Representatives, the Senate has since declined to adopt further Iran war powers resolutions in any form, with reporting indicating the Trump administration has exerted pressure on Senate Republicans to oppose them. Just last week, the Senate again voted down a concurrent resolution on the Iran war, with Sen. Thom Tillis stating, “this one doesn’t go to the president, so it’s just a statement from Congress. I’ve made that statement.”

Much of the commentary around these resolutions has framed Congress as fighting to claw back its constitutionally-envisioned powers through the only mechanism available in a Republican-led Congress. Those who have introduced their own Iran war powers resolutions — and there are many — have spoken of their desires to “reassert Congress’ constitutional authority,” and have Congress do “its job under the Constitution.”

But do they really mean this? In addition to the power to declare war, the Constitution also gives Congress the power of the purse. Upon taking the majority in the 120th Congress, Democratic leaders could insert provisions into appropriations bills that prohibit the use of funds for continued warfare in Iran. That is certainly not without precedent: Prior excursions became so unpopular that Congress utilized its power of the purse to force termination, as it did regarding Vietnam and Cambodia in 1973, Angola in 1976, and Somalia in 1993. Of course, Congress could also simply refuse either in the lame duck or new Congress to approve the supplemental war funding President Donald Trump has requested.

The new Democratic majority could also explore a court challenge against Trump’s defiance of its successfully passed Iran war powers resolution. After all, federal courts have never explicitly said that Chadha’s ruling applies to the War Powers Resolution, and there is an intriguing argument that, as distinct from other unconstitutional legislative vetoes that delegate statutory authority, the War Powers Resolution simply enforces what the Constitution already makes clear.…

Source: War on the Rocks | Published: 2026-11-25 08:30 UTC | Difficulty: 80/100

Original link: https://warontherocks.com/does-congress-really-want-its-war-powers-back/

item.title: Bangladesh’s Government Battles Unrest on Multiple Fronts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, political and social unrest

On November 18, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman asked his rivals in parliament to stand together as they had in 2024, when a student uprising ousted Sheikh Hasina from power. He also invited the opposition leader, Shafiqur Rahman of the Jamaat-e-Islami (JI), Bangladesh’s largest Islamist party, to his parliamentary office for tea. The two spoke alone.

Five days later, Rahman met a delegation from the National Citizen Party (NCP), founded by student leaders of the uprising. His government also planned formal talks with JI.

Elsewhere in Dhaka, garment workers gathered outside their factories and demanded a rise in wages.

In February, Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won more than a two-thirds majority in parliament. He is in a position to get legislation passed in parliament without the support of the opposition.

So why is he seeking his rivals’ help now?

On November 17, the day before his speech, a crowd stormed and set fire to a police station in Gopalganj, Hasina’s home district. Wage protests across the country halted production at nearly 450 garment factories that day. Rahman accused Hasina’s Awami League (AL) of encouraging violence in the factories.

Hasina’s possible return from India to Bangladesh came up even during a prayer in parliament. On November 9, after parliamentarians stood in silence to mourn former lawmakers, prominent figures, and accident victims, State Minister for Religious Affairs Mohammad Shamim Kaiser prayed to God for strength to resist any attempts to bring back “fascism.”

He meant Hasina and her party. That day, her lawyers applied for a passport at Bangladesh’s mission in New Delhi. She had fled to India on August 5, 2024.

However, Dhaka refused Hasina’s passport request. The AL, whose political activities remain banned, called a nationwide shutdown for November 19. The disruption was greatest in the party’s southern strongholds. In Gopalganj, a crowd stormed Tungipara Police Station on November 17. Witnesses said the attackers freed detained members of the AL’s student wing, and set part of the building on fire. The home of one BNP lawmaker was torched later that evening. Two days later attackers set fire to Muksudpur Police Station and the home of another BNP lawmaker.

In the southern district of Pirojpur, a 25-year-old bus assistant named Mohammad Siam died when someone set fire to the parked bus where he was sleeping. Police said they did not know who torched the bus. Nationwide, police have recorded 83 arson attacks on vehicles and crude bomb blasts at 87 sites over the past two weeks.

Grameen Bank reported attacks, including attempted arson, at 72 of its offices across 40 districts this month. Its founder, Muhammad Yunus, led the interim government after Hasina’s government fell. Rahman’s government accused AL leaders abroad of encouraging the violence.

On November 24, Hasina again asked Dhaka to fly her home from Delhi on Biman Bangladesh Airlines on December 16, which Bangladesh marks as Victory Day — the day Bangladesh’s war of independence from Pakistan ended in 1971. Hasina says she wants to surrender.

A Bangladeshi tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia last year for ordering the crackdown on protesters in July-August 2024. She denies the charges. Rahman’s government has refused the flight request, saying India would have to extradite her.

The country has also tightened security along its border with India ahead of December. Border Guards Bangladesh had stepped up patrols and installed floodlights. A commander said his force was on alert for AL supporters, who might try to enter illegally. The police chief also asked officers in border districts to watch for attempts to bring weapons or explosives into Bangladesh.

The JI and NCP share Rahman’s opposition to an AL comeback. They also want him to honor constitutional reforms voters backed in a referendum in February.

After meeting Rahman, NCP leader Nahid Islam said the current situation is not an overnight development. It was the outcome of the government’s failure to act on the deteriorating law and order situation in the country over several months.

Moreover, along with the garment sector unrest and AL-related unrest, some of the violence came from the ruling party. A Bangladeshi rights group recorded nine deaths in 35 clashes between BNP factions in October.

The Home Ministry reported fewer murder cases nationwide in the first nine months of this year than in the same period last year. In Khulna, a southern division, however, six people were killed in just over three weeks. One was a brick and sand merchant, who was shot in his shop. Local BNP leaders, including lawmakers and the city administrator, have expressed concern over the killings and extortion and called for stronger police action.

Bangladesh has deployed 101 platoons of border guards across eight districts. The Ansar paramilitary force said it had deployed 57 platoons in nine districts.

Meanwhile, garment industry workers are on strike. A sewing machine operator earning 13,500 taka a month told Human Rights Watch that rent took 6,000 and cooking gas another 2,300. The family could no longer afford the children’s schooling. “Tell me, what’s left for food?” the worker asked.

In August, a federation of garment unions asked the labor minister for a wage review. The monthly minimum wage of 12,500 taka (about $100) dates back to an agreement in 2023. The BNP had campaigned on a promise to link wages to inflation.

Workers began returning to factories after the government promised a raise from December. When a wage board meeting was postponed, they walked out again. At the end of the talks on November 23, owners were offering 15,800 taka a month. Workers’ representatives had lowered their demand from 32,000 to 22,000. The Center for Policy Dialogue, a Dhaka-based research institute, estimates it would take 16,351 taka just to buy what the minimum wage bought in 2023.…

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, political negotiation

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has challenged Andy Burnham over whether EU students in the UK could pay lower university tuition fees as part of his deal with the bloc.

The prime minister insisted the issue of tuition fees was "a separate deal", with discussions on this continuing.

Asked whether he could rule out EU students paying the same fees as British students, Burnham said this was "the European negotiating position" and "won't be put on the table".

At a UK-EU summit last Friday, the two sides agreed a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth travel scheme.

A joint statement said they would also work towards a "supplementing" agreement on tuition fees for EU students in the UK and British students in the EU, with negotiations concluding within six months.

EU sources had earlier suggested the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

But the UK has insisted the wider deal will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can reach an agreement on tuition fees.

- Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says

- Published5 days ago

At the moment, EU students at UK universities generally pay the same fees as international students, ranging from Â£11,400 to Â£38,000.

For British undergraduate students tuition fees are currently capped at Â£9,790 a year.

Universities have raised concerns that capping EU student fees at the same level could cost hundreds of millions a year, at a time when the sector is struggling financially.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Badenoch asked Burnham who would pick up the bill if EU and British students paid the same fees, "cash-strapped universities or cash-strapped taxpayers?"

In response, the PM said "the deal on tuition fees is not done", adding: "We will take that conversation forward always rightfully mindful of the challenges faced by higher education."

Pressed over whether the EU would still sign his wider deal if he refused to cut fees for European students, Burnham said legislation introduced in Parliament on Thursday would set a date for the implementation of deals on food, emissions and a youth experience scheme.

He added: "We will continue discussions with the European Union on the question of tuition fees."

Asked if he would rule out EU students paying the same tuition fees as British students, Burnham replied: "She is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position.

"That has not been put on the table. It won't be put on the table."

Asked if Burnham was saying EU students would not pay domestic fees, the prime minister minister's official spokesman told reporters he would not get ahead of the outcome of ongoing talks.

item.title: EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, trade and economic policy

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme

The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans.

The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by EU governments.

It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme.

Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move.

The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry.

The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others.

Germany and France had previously agreed a joint position under which UK involvement would have been conditional on matching EU import restrictions and tariffs on imports of Chinese electric cars and hybrids.

Alignment in this area with the EU would increase the price of increasingly popular Chinese cars in the UK, as well as raising the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on British-made cars.

'Real concern'

Now Ireland, as first reported by the Financial Times, external, is suggesting the UK could join Made in Europe without the need to match the EU's tariffs.

The argument made in favour of this is the UK and EU car industries are so heavily integrated and interdependent.

The proposal, which would also apply to Switzerland and countries in the European Economic Area (EEA) such as Norway, would depend on the non-EU countries granting the EU access to their subsidy and procurement schemes.

However, the idea is still at its early stages. It will first be discussed by EU ambassadors, before it is considered by competition ministers from the EU's member states at a meeting next month.

The proposal would also have to be accepted by the European Commission and the European Parliament.

Andy Burnham has previously pushed for UK inclusion in the scheme to avoid "collateral damage" to British industry.

Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he claimed the government had successfully "removed the threat" from the Made in Europe scheme as part of talks over the EU deals he agreed last week.

Pressed later whether he had overstated how advanced talks were on the EU side, the prime minister's spokesman said: "We continue to engage on these issues with Europe in a genuine spirit of cooperation."

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said it had proposed a "pragmatic and balanced way forward" on the scheme, having "listened closely to all member states".

item.title: Reality TV star backs extending sex education to 18
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, social policy, cultural impact

Reality TV star backs extending sex education to 18

TV celebrity and "revenge porn" victim Georgia Harrison has urged MPs to back a new law that would extend compulsory relationships and sex education (RSE) up to the age of 18.

The Only Way Is Essex and Love Island star led a protest outside Parliament to call for the change, telling the BBC it was needed to combat the "poison" young people were being exposed to online.

The demonstration comes ahead of a debate and vote next week on a draft law that would legally require all further education providers in England to teach RSE to under-18s.

The Department for Education (DfE) said it was exploring how RSE could be extended to colleges.

Compulsory relationships and sex education currently stops at age 16 in England, meaning sixth forms and colleges are not required to teach the subject.

Speaking in Westminster, Harrison said: "Between 16 and 18 is the age that people first start having sex.

"It doesn't make sense that we're abandoning them at that time."

Harrison said "misogynists" had "sold our young people advice, but really, it's poison".

"We need to undo it and the only way to undo it is through education," Harrison said.

Harrison was a victim of so-called revenge porn. Fellow reality TV performer Stephen Bear was jailed for posting intimate footage of the pair online, which he had filmed at his home in Loughton in Essex.

She said making RSE mandatory to age 18 could help prevent intimate image abuse of the kind she suffered.

The campaign outside Parliament was organised by media organisation LADbible.

The Relationships and Sex Education (Further Education Sector) Bill has been put forward by Alistair Strathern, the Labour MP for the Hitchin constituency in Bedfordshire and Hertfordshire.

It is a private members' bill, which are only debated on Fridays and rarely become law.

However, Strathern told the BBC he had "a good chance of making real change".

"I've been really encouraged by the response we've got from ministers so far," he said.

A DfE spokesperson said: "Supporting children and young people to grow up happy and healthy whilst safeguarding them from harm on and offline is a job for us all.

"We're determined that across our education system, schools and colleges play their part.

"That's why we have rolled out mandatory RHSE [relationships, sex and health education] in schools and we are exploring how we can extend this to colleges too."

The bill follows a petition by the survivor-led campaign group Make it Mandatory, which called for sex education to be mandated to 18.

Faustine Petron said she founded the campaign after surviving a coercive and abusive relationship when she was under 18.

"I thought back to the lack of education I had about the signs of abusive behaviour, grooming and coercive control," Petron said.

"I was shocked in my research to find out that sex education ends at 16. I thought 'how nonsensical'.

"I got into the relationship at 16. Why stop and have this dangerous loophole in the law?"
